lead: PID tuning is the step that turns three gains into a working controller. Trial and error is slow and unsafe on a real plant, so tuning rules measure one simple plant behaviour and compute Kp, Ti and Td. The best-known closed-loop rule is Ziegler-Nichols: raise proportional gain until the loop oscillates continuously, record that gain Ku and the period Pu, then read the settings from a table. It is used in process control, motor drives, temperature loops and any place where a plant can safely be pushed to its stability edge.
prereq: You need: Unit 2 transient response (settling time, damping) and chapter 5.2 PID structure.

sections.h3: The tuning problem and the ZN closed-loop test

blocks.text: Tuning means choosing K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>d</sub> for the plant in front of you. A gain that works on a small lab motor can saturate a furnace. Rules replace guesswork with a measured plant number.

Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning uses the loop itself. Keep integral and derivative action off: set K<sub>i</sub>=0 and K<sub>d</sub>=0, so the controller is proportional only. Apply a small set-point step. Start with low K<sub>p</sub> and increase it in small steps. After each step, watch the plant output.

items: Set the controller to P only: K<sub>i</sub>=0, K<sub>d</sub>=0.
Raise K<sub>p</sub> slowly and apply a small step.
If the output decays, raise K<sub>p</sub>. If it grows, lower K<sub>p</sub>.
At constant-amplitude oscillation, record K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub>.
Use K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub> in the ZN table, then retest.

blocks.text: At one gain the output oscillates with constant amplitude. That gain is K<sub>u</sub>, the ultimate gain. The time for one full cycle of that oscillation is P<sub>u</sub>, the ultimate period, in seconds. K<sub>u</sub> is not the normal operating gain. It is the stability-edge gain found by test. Use a small step and be ready to stop the test; many real loops cannot be pushed this far safely.
Once K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub> are known, the ZN table gives settings. For PID:

blocks.where: K<sub>p</sub> is proportional gain; K<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate gain from sustained oscillation.
T<sub>i</sub> is integral time in seconds; P<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate period in seconds.
T<sub>d</sub> is derivative time in seconds; P<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate period in seconds.
K<sub>i</sub> is integral gain in s<sup>−1</sup>; K<sub>p</sub> and T<sub>i</sub> are as above.
K<sub>d</sub> is derivative gain in s; K<sub>p</sub> and T<sub>d</sub> are as above.

blocks.text: These five numbers define the PID controller. K<sub>p</sub> sets immediate push, T<sub>i</sub> sets how fast integral action repeats the error, T<sub>d</sub> sets the derivative preview. T<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>d</sub> are times in seconds. K<sub>i</sub> is not T<sub>i</sub>; K<sub>i</sub> is K<sub>p</sub> divided by T<sub>i</sub>. K<sub>d</sub> is not T<sub>d</sub>; K<sub>d</sub> is K<sub>p</sub> times T<sub>d</sub>.
For PI control, remove derivative action:

blocks.where: K<sub>p</sub> is proportional gain; K<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate gain.
T<sub>i</sub> is integral time in seconds; P<sub>u</sub> is the ultimate period in seconds.
K<sub>i</sub> is integral gain in s<sup>−1</sup>; K<sub>p</sub> and T<sub>i</sub> are as above.

blocks.text: PI is common on noisy flow and pressure loops because derivative amplifies noise. The ZN PID rule is more aggressive and gives faster response with more overshoot.

sections.h3: Using the settings, limits and other rules

blocks.text: Set the computed gains in the controller, then test with real set-point changes and disturbances. Check overshoot, settling time and control effort. If the valve or drive saturates, reduce K<sub>p</sub> or increase T<sub>i</sub>. ZN PID is deliberately aggressive; many plants need detuning, often to about half the proportional gain or to a PI setting. A loop that cycles at the process frequency is not necessarily at K<sub>u</sub>.

The ZN closed-loop method needs a loop that can be oscillated safely. For a plant that cannot, open-loop tuning uses a recorded step response. Reaction-curve tuning fits a first-order-plus-dead-time model. Cohen-Coon uses the same step data and a different table. Those are names to recognise; this chapter computes only the ZN settings.
After tuning, record Ku, Pu and the final gains. A later mechanical change alters them. Digital PID uses the same Kp, Ti and Td but samples every T seconds; see chapter 5.8.

examples.question: A plant under proportional control oscillates continuously when K<sub>p</sub>=K<sub>u</sub>=8 and the oscillation period is P<sub>u</sub>=4 s. Find the Ziegler-Nichols PID settings K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>, T<sub>d</sub>, K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub>.
examples.answer: The ZN PID settings are K<sub>p</sub>=4.8, T<sub>i</sub>=2 s, T<sub>d</sub>=0.5 s, K<sub>i</sub>=2.4 s<sup>−1</sup> and K<sub>d</sub>=2.4 s.
examples.check:
Ku = 8
Pu = 4
Kp = 0.6 * Ku
Ti = 0.5 * Pu
Td = 0.125 * Pu
Ki = Kp / Ti
Kd = Kp * Td
print(Kp)
print(Ti)
print(Td)
print(Ki)
print(Kd)

traps: K<sub>u</sub> is the gain for sustained constant-amplitude oscillation, not the normal operating gain. A gain that only wobbles a little gives a wrong P<sub>u</sub>.
T<sub>i</sub> and T<sub>d</sub> are times in seconds. K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub> are not times; K<sub>i</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>/T<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>T<sub>d</sub>.
Measure P<sub>u</sub> after the oscillation settles, between successive peaks of the same cycle. The first transient peak gives a wrong period.
Do not mix parallel-form gains (K<sub>p</sub>, K<sub>i</sub>, K<sub>d</sub>) with series-form settings (K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>, T<sub>d</sub>) without converting.
ZN PID is aggressive. Expect overshoot; reduce K<sub>p</sub> or increase T<sub>i</sub> if the actuator saturates.

quiz.q: Define K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub> in Ziegler-Nichols closed-loop tuning.
quiz.a: K<sub>u</sub> is the proportional gain that makes the closed loop oscillate with constant amplitude. P<sub>u</sub> is the period of that oscillation in seconds.

quiz.q: Why are K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub> set to zero during the ZN closed-loop test?
quiz.a: The test needs pure proportional action. Integral action changes the oscillation and derivative action adds damping, so either would spoil the measurement of K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub>.

quiz.q: A loop gives K<sub>u</sub>=10 and P<sub>u</sub>=6 s. Find the ZN PID settings K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub>, T<sub>d</sub>, K<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>d</sub>.
A loop gives K<sub>u</sub>=8 and P<sub>u</sub>=4 s. Find the ZN PI settings K<sub>p</sub>, T<sub>i</sub> and K<sub>i</sub>.
A ZN-tuned PID loop overshoots heavily and the actuator saturates. What should you change?
quiz.a: Reduce K<sub>p</sub>, increase T<sub>i</sub>, or reduce or remove derivative action. Retune as PI if the plant is noisy. Check saturation and rate limits before judging the gains.

quiz.q: Why must P<sub>u</sub> be measured after steady oscillation, not from the first peak?
quiz.a: The first peaks belong to the transient. The period and amplitude settle later. Using the first peak gives a wrong P<sub>u</sub> and therefore wrong settings.

quiz.q: Why does using a gain that produces only a small oscillation as K<sub>u</sub> give bad PID settings?
quiz.a: Small oscillation means the gain is below the true ultimate gain. K<sub>u</sub> is too low and P<sub>u</sub> may be wrong, so the table gives gains that are too small and a response that is too slow.

beyond: Not for the exam. Relay-feedback auto-tuning replaces the manual ultimate-gain test: a relay switches the plant and the resulting limit cycle gives K<sub>u</sub> and P<sub>u</sub>. Software in PLCs and drives uses this plus model-based rules and optimization. Modern curricula add anti-windup, derivative filtering and robustness margins. Search for relay auto-tuning, Åström-Hägglund, and PID robustness.
